claims.title: The county of Vaduz takes shape
claims.summary: A separate county of Vaduz emerged in the fourteenth century in the upper Rhine valley, alongside the smaller lordship of Schellenberg, both small and often impoverished holdings within the Holy Roman Empire.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)

claims.title: The House of Liechtenstein raised to princely rank
claims.summary: Karl von Liechtenstein received the hereditary dignity of an imperial prince in 1608, confirmed for his brothers soon after, raising the wealthy Austrian dynasty to the highest rank of the nobility.

claims.title: Hohenems debts open the way
claims.summary: The counts of Hohenems, who held Vaduz and Schellenberg, fell into heavy debt, leaving the small Rhine territories available for sale to a buyer rich enough to redeem them.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)

claims.title: Purchase of the lordship of Schellenberg
claims.summary: Prince Johann Adam Andreas I bought the lordship of Schellenberg from the indebted Hohenems, the first of the two acquisitions that would form the principality; the prince did not attend the homage ceremony in person.

claims.title: Purchase of the county of Vaduz
claims.summary: Johann Adam Andreas I acquired the county of Vaduz, and from this time Vaduz Castle entered the possession of the princes of Liechtenstein, completing the territory of the future principality.

sources.label: The History of the Princely House of Liechtenstein

claims.title: Foundation of the Principality of Liechtenstein
claims.summary: Emperor Charles VI united Schellenberg and Vaduz and raised them to an Imperial Principality named Liechtenstein, granting the family the immediate standing and Diet seat it had sought; the founding diploma survives in the Princely Collections.

claims.title: A prince visits at last
claims.summary: Prince Alois II became the first reigning prince to set foot in Liechtenstein, more than a century after its foundation, the dynasty having until then governed entirely from its Austrian and Bohemian seats.

claims.title: Sovereignty through the Confederation of the Rhine
claims.summary: On the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire, Liechtenstein was admitted to Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine, gaining recognised sovereignty and surviving the Napoleonic reordering of Germany.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)
The History of the Princely House of Liechtenstein

claims.title: Membership of the German Confederation
claims.summary: After Napoleon's defeat, Liechtenstein joined the German Confederation created at the Congress of Vienna, remaining within it until 1866 while keeping close dynastic ties to Austria.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)

claims.title: First constitution and the Landtag
claims.summary: A constitution granted in 1862 established a parliament, the Landtag, beginning the slow growth of constitutional and representative institutions alongside the prince.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)

claims.title: Full independence
claims.summary: When the German Confederation dissolved after the Austro-Prussian War, Liechtenstein became a fully sovereign and independent state, its links thereafter resting on treaty and choice rather than confederation.

sources.label: Liechtenstein: History (Alpine, Principality, Sovereignty)

claims.title: Abolition of the army and neutrality
claims.summary: Liechtenstein disbanded its small military force as too costly and committed itself to permanent neutrality, a policy it has maintained through every subsequent European conflict.

sources.label: The History of the Princely House of Liechtenstein

claims.title: Liberal constitution of 1921
claims.summary: Following the First World War, Liechtenstein adopted a new constitution that combined the prince with an elected Landtag and instruments of direct democracy, modernising the state as it reoriented toward Switzerland.

sources.label: The History of the Princely House of Liechtenstein

claims.title: Customs union with Switzerland and the Swiss franc
claims.summary: A customs treaty signed in 1923 and in force from 1 January 1924 joined Liechtenstein and Switzerland into a single customs and economic area; Liechtenstein adopted the Swiss franc, binding its economy to its western neighbour.

claims.title: A prince moves to Vaduz
claims.summary: Prince Franz Josef II became the first reigning prince to take up permanent residence in Liechtenstein, ending more than two centuries of rule from abroad on the eve of the Second World War.

claims.title: Confiscation under the Beneš decrees
claims.summary: Czechoslovakia confiscated the vast Bohemian and Moravian estates of the House of Liechtenstein under the Beneš decrees, treating the family as German; the seized land, around 1,600 square kilometres, far exceeded the area of the principality.

claims.title: Women's suffrage introduced
claims.summary: By a referendum of male voters carried by a narrow margin, Liechtenstein granted women the right to vote in national elections, becoming the last country in Europe to do so.

claims.summary: Liechtenstein was admitted as the 160th member state of the United Nations, marking the small principality's full emergence as a recognised actor in international affairs.

claims.title: Constitutional referendum expands the prince's powers
claims.summary: Voters approved Prince Hans-Adam II's constitutional revision, enlarging the reigning prince's powers including a veto over legislation and the right to dismiss the government, after he threatened to leave the country.

claims.title: ICJ judgment in Liechtenstein v. Germany
claims.summary: In Certain Property (Liechtenstein v. Germany), brought to the International Court of Justice in 2001 over a confiscated van Laer painting, the Court ruled on 10 February 2005 that it had no jurisdiction, locating the dispute's source in the 1945 Beneš-era confiscations.

claims.summary: After more than six decades without recognition arising from the 1945 confiscations, Liechtenstein and the Czech Republic established diplomatic relations in 2009 and created a joint commission of historians.
